When the Yongle Emperor came to the throne, he personally reviewed the armies on five northern campaigns.
When the Yongle Emperor came to the throne, he personally led five northern campaigns and at times reviewed the imperial armies himself.
五駕北征 is five personally led northern expeditions and 六師嘗自較閱 a separate statement that he reviewed the armies himself; the rendering fuses the two.
Merit against Yunnan tribal rebels ranked below that against the wokou.
Merit for capturing or beheading Yunnan tribal rebels was ranked the same as merit against the wokou.
視倭功 means "treated like/equal to wokou merit"; "ranked below" reverses the sense.
Yunnan barbarian bandits—merit for capture and beheading ranked below Japanese pirate merit.
Yunnan barbarian bandits—merit for capture and beheading was treated the same as Japanese pirate merit.
視 means "to be judged by the standard of"; the source does not say it ranked below.
A man killed in action earned one substantive rank for his unit and one for his son.
For a man killed in action, the soldier himself (through his son) was granted one substantive rank.
本軍及子實授一秩 grants one substantive rank to the fallen soldier (and his son as heir); "his unit" is a misreading of 本軍 (the soldier himself).
Those killed in battle—the soldier's unit and his son each receive one substantive rank.
Those killed in battle—the soldier himself and his son receive one substantive rank.
本軍 here means "the soldier himself", not his unit; no double award is stated.
Assistants in the kill, and all men from the fourth rank upward, received cash reward instead.
Assistants in the kill, and those whose tally reached four heads or more, received cash rewards instead.
四級以上 refers to four or more heads (級 = head counted), not the fourth rank; the preceding rule caps promotion at three ranks.
Followers and those at the fourth rank and above all receive monetary reward.
Followers and those with four heads and above all receive monetary reward.
級 in this head-count statute means an enemy head, not a rank grade.

In the Chongzhen period, Li Zicheng and Zhang Xianzhong were purchased for ten thousand gold, ennobled as marquises; other bandits at varying rates—because bandit strength was great, normal standards were altered.

In the Chongzhen period, a bounty of ten thousand gold and enfeoffment as marquis was offered for Li Zicheng and Zhang Xianzhong; other bandits at varying rates—because bandit strength was great, normal standards were altered.
購闖、獻以萬金，爵封侯 offers a bounty and a marquisate to whoever captured them; the rebels were not purchased or ennobled.
The abuse of over-provisioning had reached its zenith.
The abuse of false and inflated merit claims had reached its extreme.
冒濫 means fraudulent and excessive (reward) claims, not over-provisioning.
Twenty years on, at Zhang Fu's urging, additional pieces were posted to the Shanxi garrisons of Datong, Tiancheng, Yanghe, and Shuozhou for frontier defense.
In the twentieth year (of Yongle), at Zhang Fu's urging, additional pieces were posted to the Shanxi garrisons of Datong, Tiancheng, Yanghe, and Shuozhou for frontier defense.
二十年 continues the Yongle 10 entry and means the twentieth regnal year (1422), not twenty years later (which would fall after the Yongle reign).
They served defense far better than open field combat.
The large pieces were best for defense, the small ones for battle.
大利於守，小利於戰 contrasts large guns (good for defense) with small guns (good for combat); it does not say they were poor in battle.
They greatly favored defense and little favored battle.
The large favored defense; the small favored battle.
大 and 小 refer to the large and small guns of s0207, not to degree.

In the second year, Ministry of Personnel Director Li Xian called for war wagons one zhang five feet long and six feet four inches high, boarded on every side with gun-ports and narrow windows aloft, each vehicle claiming ten paces fore and aft.

In the second year, Ministry of Personnel Director Li Xian called for war wagons one zhang five feet long and six feet four inches high, boarded on every side with gun-ports and narrow windows aloft, each vehicle occupying five paces front to back.
每車前後佔地五步 states five paces, not ten.
Twenty supply wagons ringed the formation, five to a face, bearing Great General pieces of every size for wood-gathering and forage, all kept inside the enclosure.
Twenty supply wagons ringed the formation, five to a face, bearing large and small General guns; transport and wood-gathering were all carried out inside the enclosure.
轉輸樵採，皆在圍中 describes transport and wood-gathering done inside the ring; the guns were not "for wood-gathering and forage".

Bowyer Zhou Sizhang argued that the Shenji musket could not be fired in quick succession and proposed a cart bearing twenty pieces and six hundred bolts, five gun-stands on the bow, one man pushing, two steadying, and one tending the match.

Arrow-maker Zhou Sizhang argued that the Shenji musket could not be fired in quick succession and proposed a cart bearing twenty pieces and six hundred bolts, five gun-stands on the bow, one man pushing, two steadying, and one tending the match.
箭工 is an arrow-maker (fletcher), not a bowyer.
The Hongwu Emperor posted four hundred vessels at Xinkou.
The Hongwu Emperor posted four hundred vessels at Xinjiangkou.
新江口 is Xinjiangkou; the character 江 has been dropped from the place name.
The Founding Emperor at Xinkou established four hundred ships.
The Founding Emperor at Xinjiangkou established four hundred ships.
新江口 is Xinjiangkou; "Xinkou" omits 江.
Hongzhi 15 brought Shaanxi Grand Coordinator Qin Geng's single-wheeled Total Victory cart—one zhang four feet long, six fighters aboard, built to smash through enemy ranks.
Hongzhi 15 brought Shaanxi Supreme Commander Qin Hong's single-wheeled Total Victory cart—one zhang four feet long, six fighters aboard, built to smash through enemy ranks.
秦紘 is read Qin Hong (紘 hóng), not Qin Geng; 總制 is a supreme commander, not a grand coordinator (巡撫).

In the fifteenth year of Hongzhi, Qin Gang, grand coordinator of Shaanxi, requested the use of single-wheel chariots called Total Victory, one zhang and four feet long, with six men above and below, able to charge enemy formations.

In the fifteenth year of Hongzhi, Qin Hong, supreme commander of Shaanxi, requested the use of single-wheel chariots called Total Victory, one zhang and four feet long, with six men above and below, able to charge enemy formations.
秦紘 is read Qin Hong; 總制 means supreme commander rather than grand coordinator.
In the twentieth year, Xuan-Datong Grand Coordinator Yu Zijun formed an army of five hundred wagons, ten men to each, the intervals studded with abatis.
In the twentieth year, Xuan-Datong Supreme Commander Yu Zijun formed an army of five hundred wagons, ten men to each, the intervals studded with abatis.
宣大總督 is the Supreme Commander of Xuanfu and Datong; grand coordinator translates 巡撫.

In the fifteenth year, Grand Coordinator Liu Tianhe renewed praise for the Total Victory cart with modest revisions—four men to haul it, its armament of guns, bows, blades, and shields reckoned at a hundred and fifty jin.

In the fifteenth year, Supreme Commander Liu Tianhe renewed praise for the Total Victory cart with modest revisions—four men to haul it, its armament of guns, bows, blades, and shields reckoned at a hundred and fifty jin.
總制 designates a supreme commander (regional military governor-general), not a grand coordinator (巡撫).
He further ordered the Feixiong, Guangwu, and Yingwu guards to raise one horse per five armies; foals born each year were sent to the capital at one year old.
He further ordered the Feixiong, Guangwu, and Yingwu guards to raise one horse per five soldiers; foals born each year were sent to the capital at one year old.
五軍養一馬 means every five soldiers kept one horse; 軍 here is "soldier", not "army".
Again he ordered the three guards of Feixiong, Guangwu, and Yingwu: five armies reared one horse; horses yearly bore foals; at one year they were sent to the capital.
Again he ordered the three guards of Feixiong, Guangwu, and Yingwu: five soldiers reared one horse; horses yearly bore foals; at one year they were sent to the capital.
軍 here denotes individual soldiers (cf. 每軍飼種馬一 in s0370).
When the Hongwu Emperor first established his capital at Nanjing, he ordered the people of Yingtian, Taiping, Zhenjiang, Luzhou, Fengyang, Yangzhou, and the prefectures of Chu and He to raise horses.
When the Hongwu Emperor first established his capital at Nanjing, he ordered the people of Yingtian, Taiping, Zhenjiang, Luzhou, Fengyang, Yangzhou, and the departments of Chu and He to raise horses.
滁、和二州 are departments (zhou), distinct from the six prefectures (府) just listed.

At first, when the Founding Emperor made Nanjing his capital, he ordered the six prefectures of Yingtian, Taiping, Zhenjiang, Luzhou, Fengyang, and Yangzhou and the two prefectures of Chu and He to pasture horses for the people.

At first, when the Founding Emperor made Nanjing his capital, he ordered the people of the six prefectures of Yingtian, Taiping, Zhenjiang, Luzhou, Fengyang, and Yangzhou and the two departments of Chu and He to pasture horses.
令…民牧馬: the people of these units were ordered to pasture horses; 州 are departments, not prefectures.

Then Esen invaded, seized twenty thousand horses, and had them boarded near the capital for the Corps Camps' cavalry drill, while all the former breeding stock was assigned to Yongping and other prefectures.

Then Esen invaded; twenty thousand horses were requisitioned and boarded near the capital for the Corps Camps' cavalry drill, while all the former breeding stock was assigned to Yongping and other prefectures.
The court, not Esen, took the 20,000 horses and boarded them near the capital for the Ming Corps Camps (團營); Esen is only the occasion.

Then Esen invaded, took twenty thousand horses, and had them boarded near the capital to mount and drill the Corps Camps, while all the former breeding stock was given to Yongping and other prefectures.
Then Esen invaded; twenty thousand horses were taken and boarded near the capital to mount and drill the Corps Camps, while all the former breeding stock was given to Yongping and other prefectures.
Subject of 取馬二萬，寄養近京 is the Ming court, which boarded the horses for its own Corps Camps.
He was promoted to grand coordinator while continuing to oversee horse policy.
He was promoted to supreme commander while continuing to oversee horse policy.
總制 is a supreme commander (regional governor-general), not a grand coordinator (巡撫).
He was transferred to grand coordinator while still supervising horse policy.
He was transferred to supreme commander while still supervising horse policy.
總制 = supreme commander, not grand coordinator.
Yiqing audited the registers and recovered more than 128,000 qing of wasteland, and opened nearly 2,900 qing for the Wu'an pasture.
Yiqing audited the registers and recovered more than 128,000 qing of wasteland, and opened more than 2,900 qing for the Wu'an pasture.
二千九百餘頃 means "more than 2,900 qing"; 餘 does not mean "nearly".

For Yansui's thirty-six camps and forts alone, from Hongzhi 11 through the next decade, the Imperial Stud spent more than 280,000 taels to buy and replace nearly 49,000 horses—and that does not include Ningxia, Datong, Juyong Pass, or the other sectors.

For Yansui's thirty-six camps and forts alone, from Hongzhi 11 through the next decade, the Imperial Stud spent more than 280,000 taels to buy and replace more than 49,000 horses—and that does not include Ningxia, Datong, Juyong Pass, or the other sectors.
四萬九千餘匹 means "more than 49,000"; 餘 does not mean "nearly".

In Jiajing 1 Lu Bi, vice director of Shaanxi pasture horses, submitted a detailed horse-policy plan: collect arrears, enforce branding, train veterinarians, and equalize land assignments to stave off immediate collapse, while opening new pastures and building reserves for the long term.

In Jiajing 1 Lu Bi, vice director of the Shaanxi Pasturage Court, submitted a detailed horse-policy plan: collect arrears, enforce branding, train veterinarians, and equalize land assignments to stave off immediate collapse, while opening new pastures and building reserves for the long term.
陝西苑馬少卿 is the vice director of the Shaanxi Pasturage Court (苑馬寺).

Jiajing 1: Vice Director of Shaanxi Pasture Horses Lu Bi submitted a detailed plan on horse policy, requesting supervision of arrears, clear branding, medical training, and equalized land assignments—to save the present—while opening pastures and broadening reserves as a long-term plan.

Jiajing 1: Vice Director of the Shaanxi Pasturage Court Lu Bi submitted a detailed plan on horse policy, requesting supervision of arrears, clear branding, medical training, and equalized land assignments—to save the present—while opening pastures and broadening reserves as a long-term plan.
苑馬 refers to the Pasturage Court (苑馬寺).
Director Tu Guoding argued: "Our ancestors made the people raise horses solely to mount and drill the capital garrisons and defend the throne—not to supply the frontiers.
Director Tu Guoding argued: "Our ancestors made the people raise horses solely to mount and drill the capital garrisons and defend the capital—not to supply the frontiers.
防護都城 means protecting the capital city, not the throne.
The pasture lands of the Nanjing guards had also long lain fallow. Minister of War Zhang Jin asked that they be restored.
The pasture lands of the Nanjing guards had also long lain fallow. Minister of War Zhang Ying asked that they be restored.
張鎣 is read Zhang Ying (鎣 yíng); "Jin" is a misreading.
Nanjing various guards' pastures also long abandoned—Minister of War Zhang Jin requested restoring them.
Nanjing various guards' pastures also long abandoned—Minister of War Zhang Ying requested restoring them.
張鎣 is read Zhang Ying (鎣 yíng).

Soon afterward, finding the stretch from Shunshheng River to Sanggan River—more than 130 li of fine grass and water—the court assigned a thousand Imperial Stud riders and a hundred soldiers of Huailai Guard to graze the land in shifts. The herd later grew to twelve thousand horses.

Soon afterward, finding the stretch from Shunsheng River to Sanggan River—more than 130 li of fine grass and water—the court assigned a thousand Imperial Stud riders and a hundred soldiers of Huailai Guard to graze the land in shifts. The herd later grew to twelve thousand horses.
Typo in the romanization of 順聖川 (Shunsheng).

Soon, as from Shunshheng River to Sanggan River over one hundred thirty li the water and grass were fine, ordered one thousand Imperial Stud riders, ordered one hundred Huailai Guard soldiers to pasture separately—later increased to twelve thousand horses.

Soon, as from Shunsheng River to Sanggan River over one hundred thirty li the water and grass were fine, ordered one thousand Imperial Stud riders, ordered one hundred Huailai Guard soldiers to pasture separately—later increased to twelve thousand horses.
Typo in the romanization of 順聖川 (Shunsheng).
Grand Coordinator Wang Chonggu purchased more than seven thousand horses for a price of more than ninety-six thousand taels.
Supreme Commander Wang Chonggu purchased more than seven thousand horses for a price of more than ninety-six thousand taels.
總督 is a supreme commander (governor-general), not a grand coordinator (巡撫).
Grand Coordinator Wang Chonggu traded for more than seven thousand horses, at a price of more than ninety-six thousand.
Supreme Commander Wang Chonggu traded for more than seven thousand horses, at a price of more than ninety-six thousand.
總督 = supreme commander, not grand coordinator.
Under Jiajing, horse markets opened at Datong, and the Xuan and other Shaanxi frontier commands soon followed.
Under Jiajing, horse markets opened at Datong, and the Shaanxi frontier and the Xuanfu command soon followed.
陝邊宣鎮 lists the Shaanxi frontier and the Xuan(fu) garrison; Xuanfu is not a Shaanxi command.
Smuggling private tea was a capital crime—no mercy even for the emperor's kin by marriage.
Smuggling private tea was a capital crime—no mercy even for meritorious nobles or imperial in-laws.
勳戚 covers both meritorious nobles (勳) and imperial relatives by marriage (戚).
